pages.title: Design current, Ib
pages.for: The current the circuit carries in normal service. You choose the protective device and the cable from it. Every later check starts from there.
pages.rule:
Single-phase: Ib = P ÷ (U × eff × pf)
Three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf)

P is the output in watts.
U is the voltage at the board if you are given one. Otherwise use 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.
A plain heater is worked with eff and pf both as 1. For a motor, take them from the nameplate or the maker's data.
In delta, each winding carries the line current ÷ √3.

traps.text: Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A where the load draws 41.48 A.
Using 230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given.
Treating diversity as a rule. It is guidance, from the On-Site Guide.

pages.where: The formula sheet and the design flowchart, step 1. Diversity figures: the On-Site Guide, Appendix A.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A 20 kW three-phase heater on a 400 V supply, power factor 1, efficiency 100%. What is its design current, Ib?
pages.alt: 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A The other two are the usual slips. 50.00 A leaves out √3. 86.96 A works it at 230 V.
pages.html:
20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A

The other two are the usual slips. 50.00 A leaves out √3. 86.96 A works it at 230 V.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Design current, [[Ib]], is the current a circuit carries in normal service. You choose the protective device and the cable from it. Every later check starts from there.
pages.alt: THE RULE Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz The design current is no more than the device's rating. The rating is no more than what the cable can carry. If it is skipped or wrong: every later step starts from the wrong current.
pages.html:
The rule

Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz

The design current is no more than the device's rating. The rating is no more than what the cable can carry.

If it is skipped or wrong: every later step starts from the wrong current.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: The cable carries what the load [[draws from the supply]], not what it gives out. The rule starts from P, the load's output. It divides by the [[efficiency]] to add the losses back. Reactance adds to the draw too, so it also divides by the [[power factor]].
pages.alt: The same 20 kW output at 400 V. Output 20.00 kW Input = output ÷ efficiency 22.99 kW Apparent = input ÷ power factor 28.74 kVA Ib, from the apparent power 41.48 A 28.74 kVA × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400) Losses stretch the input past the output. Reactance stretches the apparent power past the input. The line current follows the apparent power. It is 12.61 A more than the output alone needs. If it's skipped: the cable is sized on 28.87 A when the load draws 41.48 A. That puts the circuit's operation and safety at risk. Real, apparent and reactive power get their own lesson in AC circuits, lesson 8.
pages.html:
The same 20 kW output at 400 V.

With efficiency and power factor both at 1, nothing is lost and nothing extra is drawn. The cable carries the output's own current.Losses stretch the input past the output. Reactance stretches the apparent power past the input. The line current follows the apparent power. It is 12.61 A more than the output alone needs.Losses inside the load stretch the input past the output. At power factor 1, the apparent power is the input. The line current follows the apparent power. It is 12.61 A more than the output alone needs.Nothing is lost, but reactance stretches the apparent power past the input. The line current follows the apparent power. It is 12.61 A more than the output alone needs.
If it's skipped: the cable is sized on 28.87 A when the load draws 41.48 A. That puts the circuit's operation and safety at risk.If it's skipped: with both at 1, nothing changes. Below 1, the cable would be sized on 28.87 A while the load draws more. That puts the circuit's operation and safety at risk.

Real, apparent and reactive power get their own lesson in AC circuits, lesson 8. Here they only show where the extra current comes from.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A 7.5 kW three-phase motor on a 400 V supply, power factor 0.85, efficiency 90%. What is Ib?
pages.why: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf). 7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85) = 14.15 A. Leave out the efficiency and you get 12.74 A. Leave out the power factor and you get 12.03 A.
pages.html: 7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85) = 14.15 A

pages.name: The voltage at the board
pages.text: Work Ib at the voltage at the board. If you are given that voltage, use it. At a sub-board it is lower than 400 V, because the submain drops some on the way. We assume the load still takes its full power there. So the lower voltage means more current. That is near enough for a motor driving its load. A plain heater really draws a little less, so its figure errs on the safe side.
pages.alt: MDB 400 V submain voltage drop Sub-board 393 V final circuit 20 kW load Worked at 400 V 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A Worked at the board's 393 V 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A Diversity is guidance, not a rule, and you need not apply it. For domestic lighting, the On-Site Guide allows 66%. So ten 100 W lamps may be designed at 10 × 100 × 0.66 = 660 W rather than 1000 W. Lesson 2 covers it in full.
pages.html:
Worked at 400 V20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A

Worked at the board's 393 V20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: Here is one 20 kW load worked three ways, one step at a time.
pages.alt: 20 kW at 400 V √3 × 400 = 692.82 20 000 ÷ 692.82 = 28.87 A The same at power factor 0.8 and efficiency 87% √3 × 400 = 692.82 × 0.87 × 0.8 = 482.20 20 000 ÷ 482.20 = 41.48 A The same at a 393 V sub-board √3 × 393 = 680.70 20 000 ÷ 680.70 = 29.38 A You may see 28.86 A and 41.47 A printed elsewhere. Those are cut short, not rounded. The answer is the same.
pages.html:
20 kW at 400 V

√3 × 400 = 692.82

20 000 ÷ 692.82 = 28.87 A

The same at power factor 0.8 and efficiency 87%

√3 × 400 = 692.82

× 0.87 × 0.8 = 482.20

20 000 ÷ 482.20 = 41.48 A

The same at a 393 V sub-board

√3 × 393 = 680.70

20 000 ÷ 680.70 = 29.38 A

You may see 28.86 A and 41.47 A printed elsewhere. Those are cut short, not rounded. The answer is the same.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V.
pages.why: A model answer: The submain from the main board drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V. We assume the load takes the same power there. Since Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U), a lower voltage gives a larger current. For example, 20 kW is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V. The device and the cable are chosen so that Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. Worked at 400 V, both would be picked on too small a current. A plain heater really draws a little less, so for a heater the figure errs on the safe side.
